title: A large-scale comparison of human-written versus ChatGPT-generated essays
extended_summary:
This paper asks how well ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 can write argumentative student essays, how these AI-generated essays compare with human-written essays, and which linguistic features distinguish them. The authors frame the study as important for education because generative AI may change how homework and writing are assessed, and because educators need evidence about the quality and structure of AI-generated text.

The study used 90 argumentative essay topics from an existing essay corpus. For each topic, the authors compared one human-written essay from an online forum used by German high-school students with essays generated by ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 using a simple zero-shot prompt. The essays were evaluated by 111 secondary-school teachers who had participated in an online training session about ChatGPT and NLG systems. Teachers rated six essays each on seven criteria covering topic relevance, logic, expressiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary and text linking, and language constructs; they also reported confidence and English self-assessment. The authors additionally computed linguistic measures such as lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, nominalization, modals, epistemic markers, and discourse markers.

The main finding is that both ChatGPT models produced essays rated significantly higher than the human-written student essays across all assessment criteria, with ChatGPT-4 outperforming ChatGPT-3 on several dimensions. The paper also finds systematic linguistic differences: AI essays were more structured, used more nominalizations, and showed different patterns in discourse markers and modality. The authors conclude that generative AI is already strong enough to affect school writing tasks and that educators should rethink homework and writing instruction, emphasizing critical evaluation, reasoning, and appropriate use of AI tools rather than simple essay production.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational comparative study with a strong multi-rater design, but it is not randomized and does not evaluate an educational intervention in K-12 classrooms. The evidence is rigorous for benchmarking generated writing quality, yet it is still a correlational/assessment study rather than a causal impact study.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests that generative AI can produce high-quality argumentative writing and may affect homework and writing instruction, but it does not test student learning gains or classroom outcomes. Its practical impact is potentially meaningful, but the direct educational effect is unclear and not measured in K-12 implementation.

interventions.use_case: zero-shot ChatGPT-generated argumentative essay writing for high-school-style essay prompts, compared against human-written student essays
human teacher evaluation of AI-generated versus human-written essays using an essay-rating rubric

finding.finding_summary: Teachers rated ChatGPT essays higher than human-written student essays on all rubric criteria for argumentative writing. Mean overall scores were 3.69 for humans, 4.36 for ChatGPT-3, and 4.68 for ChatGPT-4; differences between humans and ChatGPT were significant with medium-to-very-large effects (human vs ChatGPT-3 d=0.52 to 1.15; human vs ChatGPT-4 d=0.88 to 1.43).
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of argumentative essay quality across topic/completeness, logic/composition, expressiveness, language mastery, complexity, vocabulary/text linking, and language constructs
finding.std_deviation: Human overall SD=1.26; ChatGPT-3 overall SD=1.14; ChatGPT-4 overall SD=1.11

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT-4 outperformed ChatGPT-3 on several writing-quality dimensions, including logic/composition, vocabulary/text linking, and complexity. The reported effects were small-to-medium (d=0.45 to 0.50), with mean overall scores rising from 4.36 for ChatGPT-3 to 4.68 for ChatGPT-4.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of essay quality comparing ChatGPT-3 and ChatGPT-4 outputs
finding.study_size: n=180 AI-generated essays (90 topics per model)
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT-3 overall SD=1.14; ChatGPT-4 overall SD=1.11
